paragraphs.text: Congenital amegakaryocytic thrombocytopenia-2 (CAMT2) is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by mutations in the gene for thrombopoietin (THPO). It presents in infancy or early childhood with severe thrombocytopenia and a marked reduction of bone marrow megakaryocytes. In some patients it progresses to trilineage bone marrow failure or aplastic anemia. Unlike CAMT caused by MPL mutations, serum THPO is not markedly increased. The bone marrow failure does not respond to hematopoietic stem cell transplantation, but patients have responded to THPO receptor agonists.

paragraphs.text: Pecci et al. (2018) reported 3 sibs born to Egyptian parents who were first cousins. The proband was a boy who presented at 3.5 years of age with ecchymotic patches. On examination he had preauricular skin tags and a divergent squint of the left eye. His blood counts showed very severe thrombocytopenia, hyporegenerative anemia (reticulocyte count 22.8 x 10(9)/l), and severe neutropenia. His platelets were of normal size. The bone marrow was hypocellular with very rare immature megakaryocytes. He had recurrent epistaxis, gum bleeding, rectal bleeding, recurrent otitis media, and recurrent episodes of febrile neutropenia. There was no spontaneous or diepoxybutane-induced chromosome breakage. His brother had severe isolated thrombocytopenia at 7 months of age, with normal peripheral blood cell morphology and a markedly reduced number of bone marrow megakaryocytes without other significant abnormalities. From 1.6 years of age, the brother had recurrent spontaneous bleeding that required platelet transfusions. A third sib, a girl, appeared normal at birth. At 2 months of age she developed a hematoma at a vaccination site, and her blood counts showed anemia and severe thrombocytopenia with normal blood cell morphology. Serum THPO was 10.9 pg/ml in the proband and 14.1 pg/ml in his brother. The parents had normal blood counts. Thrombocytopenia was the only feature present in all 3 affected sibs. Because the oldest sib had trilineage marrow hypoplasia, the authors suggested that the hematologic picture worsens with age. They noted that the clinical presentation could not be distinguished from CAMT due to MPL mutations.

paragraphs.text: Capaci et al. (2023) reported a Muslim Palestinian boy born to consanguineous parents. He presented at 3.5 years of age with easy bruising and thrombocytopenia (platelet count 21 x 10(9)/L) with a normal mean platelet volume. He also had urethral stenosis and mild, occasional neutropenia. Two bone marrow biopsies showed a normocellular marrow with severe hypoplasia of megakaryocytes, a few small immature forms, and mild dyserythropoiesis, consistent with amegakaryocytic thrombocytopenia. He did not have pancytopenia or increased chromosomal breakage. His serum THPO concentration was 126 pg/mL, only slightly elevated.

paragraphs.text: In 2 sibs from a Micronesian family with autosomal recessive aplastic anemia, Dasouki et al. (2013) used whole-exome sequencing to identify a homozygous c.112C-T transition in the THPO gene. The mutation results in an arg38-to-cys (R38C) substitution in the receptor-binding domain, designated R17C when the 21-amino acid signal peptide is excluded. Both parents and 1 sib were heterozygous for the mutation, and another sib was wildtype. The THPO receptor-binding domain contains 4 conserved cysteines that form 2 disulfide bonds. In silico modeling predicted that the fifth cysteine introduced by the mutation could disrupt normal disulfide bonding and cause poor receptor binding. Medium containing the mutant THPO was 2- to 3-fold less able to sustain proliferation of THPO-dependent UT7-TPO cells, consistent with a partial loss-of-function allele.

paragraphs.text: In 3 sibs with CAMT from a consanguineous Egyptian family, Pecci et al. (2018) identified a homozygous c.355C-T transition in the THPO gene, resulting in an arg119-to-cys (R119C) substitution. No MPL variants were found in the proband. The parents were heterozygous for the mutation. It was not present in the SNP, 1000 Genomes, or ExAC databases. In transfected HEK293T cells, the R119C mutant and the previously reported R38C mutant were expressed and stable. However, their concentrations in culture supernatants were about 23-fold lower than that of wildtype THPO, suggesting that both mutations impair THPO secretion. At equal concentrations, R119C THPO induced about 50% of the wildtype proliferation of THPO-dependent UT7-TPO cells and caused defective activation of STAT5, ERK1/2, and AKT downstream of MPL. The authors predicted that R119, located in helix C of the receptor-binding domain, contributes to the low-affinity binding site for MPL.

paragraphs.text: In a Palestinian boy born to first-cousin parents who had congenital amegakaryocytic thrombocytopenia without pancytopenia, Capaci et al. (2023) identified a homozygous c.-323C-T transition in the promoter region of THPO (transcript variant 1). The variant lies 45 nucleotides upstream of the transcription start site. It was present in dbSNP but not in gnomAD. No variants were found in MPL, MECOM, HOXA11, RBM8A, or in Fanconi anemia or other bone marrow failure genes. The parents and a younger sib were heterozygous for the variant, and 2 healthy sibs were homozygous for the wildtype allele. The variant lies within predicted ETS1 and STAT4 binding sites and reduced THPO promoter reporter activity by almost 80% in HEK293T cells. paragraphs.text: In 2 sibs from a Micronesian family with autosomal recessive aplastic anemia, Dasouki et al. (2013) identified a homozygous c.112C-T transition in the THPO gene, found by whole-exome sequencing. The mutation results in an arg38-to-cys (R38C) substitution in the receptor-binding domain (R17C when the signal peptide is excluded). Both parents and 1 sib were heterozygous and had reduced platelet counts, whereas a wildtype sib had a normal platelet count. Modeling predicted that the extra cysteine disrupts disulfide bonding and receptor binding. Medium containing the mutant THPO was 2- to 3-fold less able to sustain proliferation of THPO-dependent UT7-TPO cells, consistent with partial loss of function.
